lessons.title: Speaking, signing and listening in the workshop
lessons.html:
Communication keeps the workshop safe

In a farm workshop or equipment dealership you work with mechanics, apprentices, farmers, drivers and suppliers. You talk about broken tractors, parts, safety and deadlines. Some people you work with may be Deaf and use South African Sign Language (SASL). Oral communication means speaking and listening. Signed communication means using sign language. Both are real languages and both need clear, respectful use.

Sending a clear message

  • Face the person so they can see your face, lips and hands.
  • Get their attention first: say their name, or for a Deaf person, tap their shoulder gently or wave in their view.
  • Use short sentences and the correct names for parts: 'the PTO shaft', 'the hydraulic hose', 'the left rear tyre'.
  • Point to the part or show it when you can.
  • Check understanding: 'Show me which bolt you will loosen.'

Listening and watching

  • Stop the grinder or move away from noise before an important talk.
  • Look at the person and give them your attention.
  • Do not interrupt.
  • Ask if you are not sure: 'Do you mean the front axle or the rear axle?'
  • Repeat the key points to check you have them right.

Working with a Deaf co-worker

  • Learn some basic signs used in your workshop, such as stop, danger, help, finished.
  • Agree on clear signals for warnings, such as a flashing light or a hand signal.
  • Do not shout; it does not help. Speak normally and clearly if they lip-read, or write a note.
  • If there is an interpreter, talk to the Deaf person, not to the interpreter.

Hand signals near machines

When guiding a tractor driver or a crane operator, use standard hand signals agreed on site: stop, move forward, reverse, lift, lower. Only one person should give signals, and the driver must be able to see that person at all times.

lessons.title: Changing how you communicate
lessons.html:
Adapting to the person and situation

Good communicators change their message to suit the listener, the reason and the place.

Who is the listener?

ListenerHow to adapt
A farmer bringing in a planterPolite, plain words, explain the problem and the cost clearly
A new apprenticeSlow, step by step, show and explain, check often
The workshop foremanShort report: what, where, what you need
A parts supplier on the phoneGive part numbers, model and serial numbers, spell names
A Deaf co-workerFace them, use sign, gestures, written notes

What is the purpose?

  • To instruct: give steps in order.
  • To report: give facts only.
  • To ask: be polite and clear.
  • To warn: be loud, short and direct: 'Stop! Hose under pressure!'

Using the phone

  1. Greet and say your name and the business name.
  2. Say why you are calling.
  3. Speak clearly and not too fast.
  4. Write down important details: names, numbers, prices, dates.
  5. Repeat back numbers to check them.
  6. End politely and say what will happen next.

Respect for languages

South Africa has many official languages, including SASL. If someone does not understand you, change to simpler words, use another shared language, use pictures or ask a colleague to help. Never mock someone's accent, language or disability.

Body language

Your face, hands and posture send messages too. A calm face and open hands look friendly. Rolling your eyes or turning away looks rude, even if your words are polite.

lessons.title: Group talk and solving communication problems
lessons.html:
Talking in groups

Workshops hold toolbox talks and short meetings to plan the day and talk about safety. Everyone should be able to take part.

Taking part well

  • Wait for your turn. Raise your hand if needed.
  • Keep to the topic.
  • Speak clearly so everyone can hear or see you.
  • If someone uses an interpreter, give time for the interpreting.
  • Share safety concerns. Your idea might stop an accident.
  • Respect other opinions, even when you disagree.

Giving a short talk

You may be asked to explain a task to the group, such as how to jack up a trailer safely.

  1. Say what you will talk about.
  2. Give the steps in order and show the tools.
  3. Explain the dangers and how to stay safe.
  4. Ask if there are questions.

When things go wrong

Misunderstandings happen. Fix them early:

  • If you did not understand, say so and ask again.
  • If the other person did not understand, use different words, show them or write it down.
  • If someone is angry, stay calm, listen, and speak slowly. Do not shout back.
  • If a problem cannot be solved, ask the foreman to help.

Barriers to communication

  • Noise from compressors, grinders and engines
  • Different languages
  • Hearing loss
  • Being rushed or tired
  • Not paying attention

Reduce barriers by moving to a quiet place, using hearing-safe ways to talk, learning key words in other languages and signs, and taking time to listen.

Key points

  • Face the person, get their attention and use clear, short sentences.
  • Listen without interrupting and repeat key points to check.
  • Adapt your words to the listener, the purpose and the place.
  • SASL is a real language; face a Deaf person and speak to them, not the interpreter.
  • Use agreed hand signals near machines, with one signaller only.
  • Stay calm and ask for help when communication breaks down.
